heading: From Amaravati's stupas to Golconda's diamonds
body: Andhra Pradesh's recorded history opens with the Satavahanas, a Deccan dynasty that ruled from around the 3rd century BCE into the early 3rd century CE and made Amaravati, on the Krishna river, one of the great centres of early Buddhism. The Satavahanas and, after them, the Ikshvakus patronised a distinctive local art tradition — the Amaravati School of Sculpture — whose white-limestone carvings of the Buddha's life once covered a stupa so large that 19th-century British officials mistook its ruins for a natural mound before Alexander Cunningham's team recognised what they were looking at. For nearly six centuries, from around 200 BCE, Amaravati was a pilgrimage destination on the same scale as sites in the Gangetic plain, connected by trade to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.

A thousand years later, the region's coast and interior were fought over by very different powers. The Hindu Vijayanagara Empire, based further south in Karnataka, extended its authority over the Telugu country in the 14th–16th centuries, sponsoring temples and irrigation works before its defeat in 1565 by an alliance of Deccan sultanates. One of those sultanates, the Qutb Shahi dynasty, ruled from Golconda from 1518 to 1687, growing rich on the diamond mines of the region — including, by tradition, the mines that produced the Koh-i-Noor — and building the fort and tombs that still stand outside Hyderabad. The Qutb Shahis were notable for governing a majority-Telugu Hindu population with a degree of cultural accommodation unusual among the Deccan sultanates, before the kingdom fell to the Mughals in 1687.

What follows in Andhra's history is Mughal, then Nizam, then British colonial rule via the Madras Presidency, and finally the 1953 creation of Andhra State — India's first state organised on linguistic lines — which merged with Telangana in 1956 to form the united Andhra Pradesh (split again in 2014). The places on this map trace the earlier layers: the Buddhist stupas of the Krishna river valley and the fort and tomb complexes of the Deccan sultanates.
